paragraphs.heading: What a leaf is
paragraphs.text: A leaf is one of the main outgrowths of the stem in a vascular plant. It usually grows out to the side, above the ground, and it is built for photosynthesis. All the leaves of a plant taken together are called its foliage. Most leaves look green because they contain chlorophyll, a compound that soaks up the Sun's light energy and that photosynthesis cannot do without.

paragraphs.heading: A plant that feeds itself
paragraphs.text: Green plants are autotrophic: they do not eat other living things but make their own food. They trap the energy of sunlight and use it to build simple sugars, such as glucose and sucrose, out of carbon dioxide (CO₂) and water. That process is photosynthesis. The plant can store the sugars as starch, turn them into larger molecules like proteins or cellulose, the main material of plant cell walls, or burn them in cellular respiration for energy.

paragraphs.heading: Supply lines in and out
paragraphs.text: Water climbs into the leaf from the soil through the xylem, a conducting system, in a flow called the transpiration stream. Carbon dioxide drifts in from the air through stomata, small openings in the epidermis, the leaf's outer skin. Finished sugar has to reach growing parts such as shoots and roots, and it travels as sucrose in a second tissue, the phloem. Xylem and phloem run side by side, yet they usually carry their loads in opposite directions. Inside the leaf both branch into veins, which keeps the cells doing photosynthesis close to the transport system.

paragraphs.heading: Shaped to catch light
paragraphs.text: Most leaves are broad, flat and thin. That shape puts a large surface in the light and lets light pass into the tissue to reach the chloroplasts, the parts of the cell that carry out photosynthesis. Plants arrange their leaves so they catch light well without shading one another, though there are many exceptions. In most leaves the main food-making tissue, the palisade mesophyll, lies on the upper side of the blade. The flat shape also brings the leaf into close contact with the air, which helps it cool down.

paragraphs.heading: Tiny pores that open and shut
paragraphs.text: A leaf's surface is waterproofed by a layer called the cuticle. Gases pass in and out through the stomata, which open or close to control the flow of CO₂, oxygen and water vapour. Each opening is ringed by a pair of guard cells, and the turgor pressure inside them decides whether it opens. A single square centimetre of leaf may carry anywhere from 1,000 to 100,000 stomata. The leaf is also the main place where transpiration happens, and that supplies the energy to draw water up from the roots.

paragraphs.heading: Leaves that do other jobs
paragraphs.text: Leaves differ in shape, size, texture and color from one species to the next. Many conifers carry thin needles or scales, which can help in cold places with frequent snow and frost. Leaves can also store food and water, as in succulents and bulb scales. Other leaves have become pea tendrils, protective cactus spines, or the insect traps of carnivorous plants such as Nepenthes and Sarracenia. Even the scales of gymnosperm cones and the parts of flowers are built from leaves.
